title: Eigenvalues of A^k, A^-1, A^T and Polynomials in A
quickIdea: If Av = lambda v then the same v is an eigenvector of A^k, of A^-1, of A^T, of A + cI and of any polynomial p(A), with eigenvalue lambda^k, 1/lambda, lambda, lambda + c and p(lambda).
remember: Sum of the eigenvalues = tr A and product of the eigenvalues = det A, both counted with multiplicity. These two identities answer most GATE eigenvalue questions.
A^k has eigenvalues lambda^k with the same eigenvectors; A^-1 has eigenvalues 1/lambda, defined only when A is invertible.
A^T has the same eigenvalues as A, but its eigenvectors are generally different.
p(A) has eigenvalues p(lambda) for the same eigenvectors, so A^2 + 3A has eigenvalues lambda^2 + 3 lambda, and A + cI shifts every eigenvalue by c.
det(A^k) = (det A)^k and det(A^-1) = 1/det A, because the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues.

example.prompt: A = [[1,1],[1,-1]]. Find the eigenvalues of A^13.
example.work: lambda^2 - (tr A) lambda + det A = lambda^2 - 0 lambda - 2 = 0, so lambda = sqrt2 and -sqrt2. A^13 has eigenvalues (sqrt2)^13 and (-sqrt2)^13. Since (sqrt2)^12 = 2^6 = 64, these are 64 sqrt2 and -64 sqrt2. Direct check: A^2 = 2I, so A^13 = (A^2)^6 A = 64A = [[64,64],[64,-64]], whose eigenvalues are 64 sqrt2 and -64 sqrt2.
example.answer: 64 sqrt2 and -64 sqrt2, option D of GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q.31.

gateAngle: 2025 Set 1 Q.31 asks for the eigenvalues of A^13 and 2016 Set 2 Q.6 for det((A^-1)^T). Neither needs an eigenvector: the first is the power rule, the second is the product rule followed by det(A^-1) = 1/det A and det(A^T) = det A.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: The eigenvalues of A are 1, 2 and 4. What are the eigenvalues of A^2 + 3A?
variations.why: Apply p(lambda) = lambda^2 + 3 lambda to each eigenvalue: 1+3 = 4, 4+6 = 10, 16+12 = 28. The eigenvectors stay the same, which is why the rule is safe.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does A^T have the same eigenvalues as A?
variations.answer: Because det(A^T - lambda I) = det((A - lambda I)^T) = det(A - lambda I), so the two matrices have identical characteristic polynomials.
variations.why: This is a determinant identity, not a statement about eigenvectors, and the eigenvectors of A^T really can differ from those of A.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A is 3x3 with eigenvalues 2, -1 and 3. What is det(A^2)?
variations.why: det(A^2) = (det A)^2 = (2 x -1 x 3)^2 = 36, or equivalently the product 4 x 1 x 9 of the squared eigenvalues.

trap.what: Assuming eigenvalues add or subtract under A + B, or that A and A^T share eigenvectors.
trap.why: The eigenvalue rules are one-matrix rules: they hold for powers, inverses, transposes and polynomials of a single A, and there is no rule at all for a sum of two matrices.
trap.counterexample: A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] both have eigenvalues 0, 0, but A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] has eigenvalues 1 and -1, not 0 and 0.

check.question: The eigenvalues of A are 3 and 5. What are the eigenvalues of A^-1, and of A^2 - I?
check.answer: A^-1 has 1/3 and 1/5; A^2 - I has 8 and 24.
check.explanation: The inverse rule gives 1/lambda, and the polynomial rule with p(t) = t^2 - 1 gives 9-1 = 8 and 25-1 = 24. Both hold only because A is invertible, which det A = 15 confirms.
